reading.reading_name: Guidance for Standard VI: Conflicts of Interest

drills.los_text: demonstrate a thorough knowledge of the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct by interpreting the Code and Standards in various situations involving issues of professional integrity
drills.reading_name: Guidance for Standard VI: Conflicts of Interest

questions.stem: Weiss, a research analyst at broker/investment bank Williamsburg, is writing a research report on Jimco. Williamsburg's M&A department has represented Jimco in all of its acquisitions for 20 years, and Williamsburg officers sit on the boards of Jimco subsidiaries. The most appropriate action for Weiss is to:

options.A: omit any opinion on Jimco's stock in place of disclosure.
options.B: disclose Williamsburg's special relationship with Jimco in the report.
options.C: rely on the firewall between the M&A and research departments.

rationales.A: Omitting opinions does not cure the conflict. The special relationship must be disclosed regardless of whether the report expresses a view on Jimco's stock, because the relationship itself threatens the independence and objectivity of the report writer.
rationales.B: Weiss must disclose in his research report Williamsburg's special relationship with Jimco. Broker/dealer management of and participation in public offerings must be disclosed in research reports. Because the position of underwriter to a company entails a special past and potential future relationship with a company that is the subject of investment advice, it threatens the independence and objectivity of the report writer and must be disclosed.
rationales.C: A firewall between departments does not eliminate the disclosure duty under Standard VI(A). The underwriting relationship must still be disclosed in the research report itself so that users of the report can judge the report's objectivity for themselves.

questions.stem: Dover & Roe has sold a 25% interest in its partnership to bank holding company First of New York. Immediately afterward, Hobbs raised his recommendation on First of New York from sell to buy and added its commercial paper to the approved list. Best practice for Hobbs is most likely to:

options.A: continue coverage, treating the partnership stake as too remote.
options.B: discontinue research coverage of First of New York.
options.C: recuse himself permanently from all research coverage.

rationales.A: A 25% ownership stake held by the firm creates a real conflict of interest for coverage of that company, and an upgrade from sell to buy immediately after the sale makes any claim of remoteness implausible.
rationales.B: Best practice would be for Hobbs to discontinue research coverage of First of New York because the new ownership interest in this company creates a conflict of interest. At minimum, Hobbs must disclose the new relationship with First of New York to all Dover & Roe clients. Hobbs must also require the ownership interest to be disclosed to clients by the firm's portfolio managers when they make specific investment recommendations or take investment actions with respect to First of New York's securities.
rationales.C: The remedy is targeted rather than blanket: discontinuing coverage of the conflicted name, or at minimum disclosing the new relationship to all clients and requiring portfolio managers to disclose it with recommendations and actions in that company's securities. Permanent recusal from all research is not required.

questions.stem: Fargmon recommended Kincaid Printing. His wife then inherited $3 million of Kincaid stock, and a year later Fargmon is asked to write a follow-up report on the company. The most appropriate course for Fargmon is to:

options.A: treat his wife's inherited holding as outside his own ownership.
options.B: require his wife to sell her inherited Kincaid stock.
options.C: disclose his wife's ownership to his employer and in the report.

rationales.A: A family member's holding is beneficial ownership for conflict purposes. His wife's Kincaid position creates a conflict that Fargmon must disclose rather than disregard as someone else's property.
rationales.B: Divestiture of a family member's inherited assets is not required. The remedy is disclosure of the ownership, or avoidance of the conflict by reassigning the follow-up report to another analyst.
rationales.C: At minimum, Fargmon must disclose his wife's ownership of Kincaid stock to his employer and in his follow-up report. Best practice is to avoid the conflict altogether by asking his employer to assign another analyst to draft the follow-up report.

questions.stem: Roberts speculates in penny stocks for her own account and has purchased 100,000 shares of Drew Mining at $0.30. Asked to write a report on the penny stock mining industry, she would recommend Drew as a buy in any event. The most appropriate course for Roberts is to:

options.A: disclose to her employer and consider declining the assignment.
options.B: disclose to her employer but not to readers of the report.
options.C: proceed without disclosure, since the buy rating stands on its own.

rationales.A: Roberts must disclose the conflict to her employer and should consider declining the research assignment on Drew Mining. If Roberts's employer has her write the report despite the conflict, Roberts must disclose the conflict in her report as well.
rationales.B: Internal disclosure alone is not sufficient. If the report is published, the conflict must also be disclosed in the report to clients, who otherwise cannot judge the objectivity of the recommendation.
rationales.C: The independent merit of the buy recommendation does not cure the ownership conflict. The position must still be disclosed to her employer and, if she writes the report despite the conflict, in the report itself.

questions.stem: Snead, a retirement fund portfolio manager, begins receiving a new quarterly performance bonus from her employer and, without telling her clients of the change, purchases high-beta stocks that are contrary to her clients' investment policy statements. Snead has most likely:

options.A: violated neither Standard III(C) nor Standard VI(A).
options.B: violated Standard III(C) but not Standard VI(A).
options.C: violated Standard VI(A) as well as Standard III(C).

rationales.A: A compensation change that rewards short-term performance is a conflict of interest clients must be told about, so the absence of any violation is not sustainable. Firms may pay employees based on performance, and performance bonuses are common, but the commonness of the arrangement does not remove the duty to inform clients when the arrangement changes in a way that pits the manager's pay against the objectives of their accounts. The purchases contrary to the clients' investment policy statements are a suitability failure in their own right, so neither standard is left intact.
rationales.B: Purchasing high-beta stocks contrary to the clients' investment policy statements does breach the suitability requirement, and that breach compounds the problem, but it is not the only failure. The tested violation is the nondisclosure of the changed compensation arrangement under Standard VI(A), which created the conflict that produced the unsuitable investing in the first place.
rationales.C: Snead violated Standard VI(A) by failing to inform her clients of the changes in her compensation arrangement with her employer, which created a conflict of interest between her compensation and her clients' investment policy statements. Firms may pay employees based on performance, but pressure from her employer to achieve short-term performance goals conflicts with the requirement to take only investment actions that are consistent with the objectives of Snead's accounts. The high-beta purchases contrary to the clients' investment policy statements breach the suitability requirement of Standard III(C) as well, but it is the undisclosed compensation conflict that Standard VI(A) reaches.

questions.stem: Carter, a broker/dealer representative, accepts a stock promoter's offer of additional compensation for selling Badger shares to his clients, sells them the shares, and tells neither his clients nor his employer of the promoter's offer. With respect to Standard VI(A), Carter most likely:

options.A: owed his clients disclosure of the arrangement.
options.B: owed no disclosure, the shares being suitable.
options.C: owed no disclosure, the payment being supplemental.

rationales.A: Carter violated Standard VI(A) by failing to disclose to clients that he is receiving additional compensation for recommending and selling Badger stock. At minimum, Carter must disclose the arrangement with Badger to his clients so they can evaluate whether his recommendations to buy Badger were affected by this arrangement. Best practice is for Carter to avoid this conflict of interest altogether by declining the offer of additional compensation from Badger Company.
rationales.B: Suitability does not cure hidden compensation. Even if Badger shares were an appropriate holding for the clients who bought them, the clients must know that the recommendation is being paid for by the promoter so they can evaluate whether Carter's recommendation to buy Badger was affected by that arrangement; at minimum the arrangement must be disclosed, and declining it is better practice still.
rationales.C: Outside compensation for recommending and selling a particular stock is a conflict of interest requiring disclosure, and whether it supplements or replaces the compensation Carter receives from his firm is irrelevant to that duty. Clients need the disclosure in order to judge whether the recommendation was affected by the promoter's payment, and the employer is entitled to know of the arrangement as well.

questions.stem: Papis, chief investment officer of a state retirement fund, moves the fund's real estate allocation to Accessible Real Estate, a new asset management firm founded by his business school classmate Nagle to build assets under management. Papis mentions the classmate relationship to no one at the fund, and Accessible appears in the next annual report's list of external managers. With respect to Standard VI(A), Papis most likely:

options.A: had a conflict his employer should have been told of.
options.B: had a conflict the annual report adequately revealed.
options.C: had no duty of disclosure, selection being his alone.

rationales.A: Papis violated Standard VI(A) by not disclosing to his employer his personal relationship with Nagle. Disclosure of his history with Nagle would allow his firm to determine whether the conflict may have impaired Papis's independence in deciding to change external managers.
rationales.B: An after-the-fact listing of Accessible Real Estate among the fund's external managers is not disclosure of the personal relationship to the employer, which is what Standard VI(A) requires. From the annual report the firm learns only that a manager changed, not that the new manager is a former classmate whose firm is trying to build assets under management, which is the fact that would let the firm assess whether Papis's independence was impaired.
rationales.C: Discretionary authority over the selection of external managers does not obviate the duty to disclose a personal relationship that could impair independence. That authority is the reason the disclosure matters: because no one else reviewed the decision, only disclosure of his history with Nagle would allow the firm to determine whether the conflict may have impaired Papis's independence in moving the real estate allocation.

questions.stem: Smith, an analyst at XYZ, is preparing a purchase recommendation on JNI. The circumstance Smith is required to disclose as a conflict of interest is most likely:

options.A: XYZ's substantial common stock position in JNI.
options.B: Smith's frequent purchases of JNI products.
options.C: Smith's brother-in-law's role as a JNI supplier.

rationales.A: This item involves Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts, specifically the holdings of an analyst's employer in company stock. XYZ's ownership of the stock of the company that is the subject of the research report creates a conflict of interest that must be disclosed in the research report. XYZ could instead avoid the conflict by not having Smith prepare a recommendation on JNI or on any other company in which XYZ has an ownership interest.
rationales.B: Smith's use of the products JNI produces is not a required disclosure, because it will likely not create a conflict of interest. Being a customer of the company gives Smith no interest in how the recommendation affects JNI's share price, so it is not a matter that could reasonably be expected to impair his independence and objectivity.
rationales.C: The relationship between the analyst and the company through a relative who supplies it is so tangential that it does not create a conflict of interest necessitating disclosure. The brother-in-law's business with JNI is not an interest of Smith's that could reasonably be expected to bias his recommendation, unlike his employer's own holding of the stock.

questions.stem: Jamison, a junior research analyst, is asked to write a research report on Britland, a company whose mergers and acquisitions work her employer, Howard & Howard, has handled for 20 years and two of whose subsidiaries have Howard & Howard senior officers serving as directors. Jamison's most appropriate course of action is to:

options.A: write the report, but express no opinions in it.
options.B: write no report on Britland or its subsidiaries.
options.C: write the report and disclose the director relationship.

rationales.A: Whether Jamison expresses any opinions in the report is irrelevant to her duty to disclose all conflicts of interest. Writing a purely factual report removes neither the client relationship between Howard & Howard's mergers and acquisitions department and Britland nor the director relationship created by the two senior officers, so the conflicts remain and remain undisclosed.
rationales.B: Jamison should not write the report, because the two Howard & Howard officers serve as directors for subsidiaries of Britland and because Britland has been a client of the firm for 20 years. Best practice would be to avoid the conflicts of interest by not providing a research report on companies that are clients of, or that have a director relationship with, Howard & Howard. If the conflicts are not avoided, both the client relationship and the director relationship must be disclosed by Jamison in her research report.
rationales.C: Disclosing the director relationship covers only one of the two conflicts: the 20-year client relationship between Howard & Howard's mergers and acquisitions department and Britland would also have to be disclosed. Even then, disclosure is the fallback; the better course is to avoid both conflicts by not providing a research report on the company at all.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(A), a conflict of interest is best described as:

options.A: any financial stake the member may hold in a recommended security.
options.B: any matter that could reasonably be expected to impair objectivity.
options.C: any conduct that can be shown to have harmed a client for personal gain.

rationales.A: Conflicts extend well beyond ownership of the securities being recommended. Compensation structures, board seats, referral arrangements, and personal and professional relationships all qualify, because a conflict of interest is any matter that could reasonably be expected to impair independence and objectivity or raise a question about whether actions, judgment, or decision making is free from bias.
rationales.B: A conflict of interest is any matter that could reasonably be expected to impair independence and objectivity or raise a question about whether actions, judgment, or decision making is free from bias. Conflicts of interest occur when there is a personal or professional interest that may impair a member's or candidate's ability to perform his or her professional responsibilities in an independent and objective manner. They arise often in the investment profession, and they can occur between the interests of clients, the interests of employers, and the member's or candidate's own personal interests. A common source of conflict is compensation structure, especially incentive and bonus structures that provide immediate returns for members and candidates with little or no consideration of long-term value creation.
rationales.C: The definition is prospective rather than retrospective: matters that could reasonably be expected to impair independence and objectivity qualify whether or not the member ever acts on them and whether or not any harm to a client occurs. A matter that merely raises a question about whether judgment is free from bias is already a conflict, which is why the appearance of a conflict is to be avoided along with the real thing.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(A), the best practice with respect to a conflict of interest is most likely to:

options.A: avoid the conflict altogether.
options.B: disclose the conflict fully.
options.C: mitigate the conflict with firewalls.

rationales.A: Best practice is to avoid actual conflicts of interest and the appearance of them. When it is not reasonable for members and candidates to avoid a conflict, clear and complete disclosure of the conflict is necessary. Members and candidates should also seek to mitigate the conflict to the extent possible and disclose how the conflict has been mitigated.
rationales.B: This inverts the hierarchy. Avoidance is the first-best practice, for actual conflicts and for the appearance of them alike; clear and complete disclosure becomes necessary only when it is not reasonable for the member or candidate to avoid the conflict. Full disclosure does not license taking on conflicts freely so long as they are reported.
rationales.C: Mitigation follows disclosure rather than preceding it or substituting for it. The order is to avoid the conflict; where avoidance is not reasonable, to disclose it clearly and completely; and then to seek to mitigate it to the extent possible and disclose how it has been mitigated. Firewalls are one mitigation tool, not a first step that makes disclosure unnecessary.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(A), service by investment personnel as a board member or director most likely poses:

options.A: one conflict, over the time it takes from client work.
options.B: no conflict, where the director recuses from relevant votes.
options.C: three conflicts, over divided duties, pay, and information.

rationales.A: Time taken from client work is not the concern the standard addresses. Board service poses three basic conflicts of interest: the tension between the duties owed to clients and the duties owed to the shareholders of the company, the securities or options received as compensation for serving on the board, and the opportunity to receive material nonpublic information about the company.
rationales.B: Recusal from votes involving the employer does not address any of the three basic conflicts: the tension between duties owed to clients and duties owed to the company's shareholders, the receipt of securities or options to purchase securities of the company as compensation for board service, and the opportunity to receive material nonpublic information about the company. The remedy in the guidance is to isolate investment personnel who serve as directors from those making investment decisions by firewalls or similar restrictions.
rationales.C: Service as a board member or director poses three basic conflicts of interest. First, a conflict may exist between the duties owed to clients and the duties owed to shareholders of the company. Second, investment personnel who serve as directors may receive securities or options to purchase securities of the company as compensation for serving on the board, which could raise questions about trading actions that might increase the value of those securities. Third, board service creates the opportunity to receive material nonpublic information involving the company; even though the information is confidential, the perception could be that information not available to the public is being communicated to a director's firm. When members and candidates providing investment services also serve as directors, they should be isolated from those making investment decisions by firewalls or similar restrictions.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(A), beneficial ownership of an investment most likely arises from:

options.A: the member's own accounts, but not a family member's.
options.B: a pecuniary interest, or power to vote or dispose.
options.C: legal title rather than any pecuniary interest.

rationales.A: Standard VI(A) does not stop at accounts the member holds personally. Holdings of a spouse, children, or other family members are attributed to the member whenever the member has a pecuniary interest in them, or holds the power to vote them or to direct their disposition. Treating every family account as separate by definition would let a member route conflicted positions through relatives and escape the disclosure the standard requires, which is the outcome the definition is written to prevent.
rationales.B: Standard VI(A) guidance defines the term functionally rather than by registration: members and candidates beneficially own securities or other investments if they have a direct or indirect pecuniary interest in the securities, have the power to vote or direct the voting of the shares of the securities or investments, or have the power to dispose or direct the disposition of the security or investment. Any one of those three tests is sufficient on its own. A position held through a trust, a family entity, or a joint account can therefore create beneficial ownership even though the member's name appears nowhere on the registration, and any such holding that could reasonably be expected to impair independence and objectivity must be disclosed to clients, prospective clients, and the employer.
rationales.C: Beneficial ownership turns on economic interest and control, not on legal title. The definition reaches indirect pecuniary interests as well as direct ones, and it is satisfied independently by the power to vote the shares or the power to direct their disposition. Securities held in joint accounts, trusts, and family entities therefore fall inside the definition whenever one of those tests is met, even though the member's name appears nowhere on the registration, so a title-based test would leave the most common conflicts undisclosed.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(A), disclosure of conflicts arising from nonstandard fee structures, subadvisory agreements, and mutual fund service-fee rebates is most likely required:

options.A: for institutional clients but not retail ones.
options.B: for no client of the firm.
options.C: for every client the arrangement affects.

rationales.A: The duty under Standard VI(A) runs to all affected clients, retail and institutional alike. Nothing in the standard conditions disclosure on the size or sophistication of the client; the test is whether the arrangement could reasonably be expected to impair the member's independence and objectivity or to interfere with the duties owed to the client, and a nonstandard fee structure does that whoever is paying it. A retail client is if anything less able to infer the arrangement unaided.
rationales.B: Nonstandard fee arrangements, rebates, and subadvisory economics are exactly the kind of firm-level economics that can bias recommendations, which is why the standard requires that they be disclosed to clients rather than treated as internal housekeeping. The rebate of a portion of the service fee that some classes of mutual funds charge investors is an obvious conflict: it gives the firm a direct financial reason to prefer one share class or product over another, and the client cannot weigh the recommendation without knowing it exists.
rationales.C: Standard VI(A) guidance requires that disclosures be made to clients regarding conflicts that may arise in fee arrangements, subadvisory agreements, or other situations involving nonstandard fee structures. Equally important is disclosure of arrangements in which the firm benefits directly from investment recommendations. An obvious conflict of interest is the rebate of a portion of the service fee some classes of mutual funds charge to investors. Members and candidates must disclose such relationships so that clients can fully understand the conflicts and judge the recommendation accordingly, and the duty extends to every client the arrangement touches.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(A), pressure on a sell-side analyst to write a favorable research report is most likely:

options.A: a demand the analyst must accommodate when firm revenue depends on it.
options.B: a conflict created by the analyst's own firm and by corporate issuers.
options.C: a management matter beyond the individual analyst's responsibility.

rationales.A: Yielding to issuer or internal marketing pressure for favorable research is precisely the independence failure the guidance targets. A member or candidate must resolve a situation presenting a potential conflict of interest, or disclose it in accordance with the principles of Standard VI(A). The firm's revenue interest is the source of the conflict, not a justification for acting on it, and accommodating the pressure puts a compromised report in front of clients.
rationales.B: Sell-side analysts working for broker/dealers may be encouraged, not only by members of their own firm but also by corporate issuers themselves, to write research reports about particular companies. Buy-side analysts are likely to face similar conflicts as banks exercise their underwriting and security-dealing powers. A marketing division may ask an analyst to recommend the stock of a certain company in order to obtain business from that company. The pressure therefore has two sources, one inside the firm and one outside it, and members and candidates must resolve situations presenting potential conflicts of interest or disclose them in accordance with the principles set forth in Standard VI(A).
rationales.C: The obligation is personal and cannot be handed upward. The individual analyst must address the conflict by resolving it, escalating it, or ensuring that it is disclosed. Treating the pressure as somebody else's responsibility leaves the conflicted recommendation in front of clients, which is the harm the standard exists to prevent; that the firm's management also has a duty to control such pressure does not displace the analyst's own.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(A), the mere appearance of a conflict of interest is most likely:

options.A: a problem in itself for members and their employers.
options.B: a problem no earlier than a client's first complaint.
options.C: a problem when actual, but not when merely apparent.

rationales.A: Standard VI(A) guidance states that the mere appearance of a conflict of interest may create problems for members, candidates, and their employers. Many of the conflicts the guidance describes may therefore be explicitly prohibited by an employer in order to avoid those conflicts altogether. Employers commonly restrict personal trading, outside board membership, and related activities to prevent situations that might not normally be considered problematic from a conflict-of-interest point of view but that could give the appearance of a conflict of interest. Members and candidates must comply with those employer restrictions.
rationales.B: The appearance of a conflict matters whether or not any client ever objects, so a complaint is not what turns it into a problem. That is exactly why employers impose preclearance, personal-trading, and outside-activity restrictions in advance rather than waiting to hear from a client: by the time a client raises the concern, the appearance has already done its damage to the member's and the firm's credibility.
rationales.C: This reflects the misconception that appearances are harmless until a conflict turns out to be real. The guidance says the mere appearance of a conflict of interest may create problems for members, candidates, and their employers, and that the appearance alone is enough to justify employer restrictions on activities such as personal trading and outside board membership, even where the underlying activity would not otherwise be considered a conflict.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(A), a conflict-of-interest disclosure already made to a client most likely requires updating:

options.A: when the nature of the conflict changes materially.
options.B: at no point after the initial disclosure.
options.C: not before the client asks whether it remains accurate.

rationales.A: Best practice dictates updating disclosures when the nature of a conflict of interest changes materially — for example, if the nature of a conflict of interest worsens through the introduction of bonuses based on each quarter's profits as opposed to annual profits, which shortens the horizon over which the member is rewarded and sharpens the incentive to act against the client's longer-term interest. In making and updating disclosures of conflicts of interest, members and candidates should err on the side of caution to ensure that conflicts are effectively communicated.
rationales.B: A disclosure made at the opening of the relationship describes the conflict as it then stood. Once the nature of that conflict changes materially, the original disclosure no longer tells the client what is needed to judge the member's objectivity, so best practice is to update it. An initial disclosure places the client on notice of the arrangement described, not of every arrangement that may replace it later.
rationales.C: The updating duty belongs to the member and is triggered by a material change in the nature of the conflict, not by any client inquiry. Waiting to be asked leaves the client relying on a disclosure that has become inaccurate, and members and candidates should err on the side of caution to ensure that conflicts are effectively communicated.

questions.stem: A member's conflict of interest that might be detrimental to the employer's business is most likely:

options.A: covered by Standard VI(A).
options.B: excluded from Standard VI(A).
options.C: governed by the employment contract, not the Code.

rationales.A: Standard VI(A) also deals with a member's or candidate's conflicts of interest that might be detrimental to the employer's business. Any potential conflict situation that could prevent clear judgment about, or full commitment to, the execution of a member's or candidate's duties to the employer should be avoided. If the member or candidate does not avoid the conflict, it must be reported to the employer.
rationales.B: The standard's reach is not confined to conflicts affecting clients. It expressly extends to conflicts of interest that might be detrimental to the employer's business, requires that any potential conflict capable of impairing judgment about or commitment to the member's duties be avoided, and requires that a conflict which is not avoided be reported to the employer.
rationales.C: An employment contract may add obligations, but it does not displace the Code and Standards. The duty to avoid a conflict detrimental to the employer, or else to report it to the employer, arises under Standard VI(A) itself and operates alongside whatever the contract says.

questions.stem: A research analyst withholds a buy recommendation on a stock from his employer's pension account so that he can purchase the shares personally first. His conduct is most likely:

options.A: a violation of Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis.
options.B: a personal investment he was entitled to make.
options.C: a violation of Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions.

rationales.A: The research was already complete, so diligence and reasonable basis is not the issue. The failing is one of transaction priority: he withheld a recommendation that his employer's pension account was entitled to receive in order to trade ahead of it.
rationales.B: A member may invest his own money in securities he has researched, but not ahead of the accounts he serves. Suppressing the recommendation so that he could buy at a lower price placed his personal interest ahead of his employer's, which is the conduct the priority rule forbids; his entitlement to hold the stock does not extend to buying it before the account for which he researched it.
rationales.C: He violated Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions by taking advantage of his knowledge of the stock's value before allowing his employer to benefit from that information. Client transactions must take precedence over transactions made on behalf of the member's or candidate's firm, and firm transactions over personal ones; delaying the recommendation so that he could buy first inverts that order and converts information generated for the employer into a personal gain.

questions.stem: An aggressive growth fund manager instructs her brokers to buy each hot new issue for an account held in her husband's name, and her fund's clients are unable to participate. Her conduct is most likely:

options.A: a breach of Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions.
options.B: no more than a failure to disclose the account to her clients.
options.C: a trade exempt from the priority rule.

rationales.A: She breached Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions. To comply with the standard, she must acquire shares for her mutual fund first, before acquiring them for her husband's account. She must also disclose the trading in her husband's account to her employer, because that activity creates a conflict between her personal interests and her employer's interests.
rationales.B: A disclosure is owed, but not as described and not instead of the priority breach. The disclosure the conduct calls for runs to her employer, because trading in her husband's account creates a conflict between her personal interests and the employer's. Treating the matter as no more than a disclosure lapse understates it: the core failure is routing each limited hot issue to the husband's account before the fund she manages, which inverts the order the priority rule requires whatever was disclosed to whom.
rationales.C: Trades for an immediate family member's account are personal transactions subject to the priority rule whenever the member has a beneficial interest in that account, so registration in the husband's name does not put them outside it. Her clients were left unable to participate in issues routed to that account first, which is precisely the harm the rule addresses.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager allocates each new issue to her other clients first and places whatever remains in her parents' fee-paying retirement account. Her conduct is most likely:

options.A: a prudent safeguard against favoring family.
options.B: a violation of Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions.
options.C: a violation of Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts.

rationales.A: Fee-paying family accounts are ordinary client accounts, not personal accounts to be placed last. Systematically allocating to them only what other clients leave behind disadvantages them relative to every other client of the firm and breaches the duty owed to them, so the practice is not the safe course it appears to be; even-handed allocation, not subordination, is what avoids favoritism.
rationales.B: She violated Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions by breaching her duty to her parents, treating them differently from her other accounts simply because of the family relationship. As fee-paying clients of the firm, her parents are entitled to the same treatment as any other client. If she has beneficial ownership in the account, however, and the firm has preclearance and reporting requirements for personal transactions, she may have to preclear the trades and report the transactions to the firm — a procedural obligation, not a reason to allocate to them last.
rationales.C: Nothing in the conduct described is a disclosure failure; what is described is the allocation itself. The defect is the unequal treatment of a fee-paying client, which the priority-and-fairness logic of Standard VI(B) prohibits whether or not the family relationship has been disclosed to anyone. Disclosure and preclearance duties may well attach if she has beneficial ownership in her parents' account, but satisfying them would not make allocating the leftovers to those clients acceptable.

questions.stem: An employee makes substantial gains buying stocks just before his firm adds them to its buy list, and the director responsible for monitoring personal trading never requires him to file the firm's quarterly personal transaction form. The employee's trading is most likely:

options.A: excused by the supervisor's failure to require the form.
options.B: exempt from the priority rule as it preceded the listing.
options.C: prohibited by Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions.

rationales.A: The supervisor's failure is a breach of Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors in its own right, and it does not excuse the employee. The employee violated Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions by placing personal transactions ahead of client transactions; the uncollected quarterly forms are a separate supervisory failure rather than a substitute for his own breach, and a member cannot shelter behind a control his employer failed to operate.
rationales.B: Trading on knowledge that securities are about to be added to the firm's buy list is exactly what the priority rule reaches. Buying before the formal listing is the offense, not an exemption from it: the price advantage comes from information generated for clients, and the client-destined recommendation is what makes the purchases profitable.
rationales.C: He violated Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions by placing personal transactions ahead of client transactions. In addition, the director violated Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors by not requiring him to complete the quarterly personal transaction form, but that supervisory lapse is independent of, and does not relieve, the employee's own priority-of-transactions breach.

questions.stem: At an internal video conference, analyst Wilson makes negative comments about a major insurance company, and the firm distributes the resulting report to clients the next day. Seven minutes after the conference ends, Riley, the firm's head of trading, closes the firm's long call position in the insurer and establishes a sizable put position, saying the trades were to facilitate anticipated institutional client sales. Riley's trading is most likely:

options.A: not a violation, the trades being a hedge of firm exposure.
options.B: a violation of Standard II(A), Material Nonpublic Information.
options.C: a violation of Standard VI(B), Priority of Transactions.

rationales.A: Trading for the firm's own account seven minutes after the internal conference, and a full day before clients received the report, denies customers the opportunity to act on the recommendation first. A wish to hedge the firm's own exposure, or to pre-position for anticipated institutional demand, does not override that duty: Standard VI(B) requires that the interests of clients and employers come ahead of the firm's and the member's own financial interests, and the firm had to wait until clients had an opportunity to receive and assimilate the recommendation before trading for itself.
rationales.B: The negative view aired in the internal video conference is Wilson's own research opinion, developed inside the firm, rather than material nonpublic information belonging to the insurance company. Standard II(A) governs issuer information obtained in a relationship of trust or by misappropriation; the firm's own pending, undisseminated research is addressed instead by the duty of transaction priority. The operative failure here is that the firm traded ahead of its clients, which is a Standard VI(B) matter.
rationales.C: Riley violated Standard VI(B) by not giving customers an opportunity to buy or sell in the options market before the firm itself did. By taking action before the report was disseminated, Riley's firm may have depressed the price of the calls and increased the price of the puts, so a client who later traded on Wilson's recommendation faced worse prices because of the firm's own transactions. Riley should have avoided the conflict of interest by waiting to trade for the firm's own accounts until its clients had an opportunity to receive and assimilate Wilson's recommendations. The stated purpose of facilitating anticipated institutional sales does not excuse the sequence.

questions.stem: Rose, a portfolio manager, plans to sell part of his personal portfolio to cover his child's tuition. The holding he wants to sell is a household products stock that his firm recently upgraded to a strong buy. Under Standard VI(B), Priority of Transactions, the sale is most likely:

options.A: permitted once he informs his firm of his intentions.
options.B: prohibited while the firm's strong buy rating stands.
options.C: permitted only after clients have bought the stock.

rationales.A: Standard VI(B), Priority of Transactions, does not limit transactions of company employees that differ from current recommendations, as long as the sale does not disadvantage current clients. Rose therefore remains free to sell his personal holdings for his own financial reasons, here funding tuition, once his firm has been properly informed of his intentions so that it can confirm no client is harmed and that the trade is consistent with firm policy on personal investing.
rationales.B: A personal transaction that differs from the firm's current recommendation is not barred as such. It is acceptable provided clients are not disadvantaged, and a personal liquidity need such as tuition is exactly the circumstance the guidance contemplates. Rose does not prosper from an inflated recommendation merely by selling into a market in which his firm is recommending purchase; what would be impermissible is a sale that took priority over, or worsened the execution of, client transactions.
rationales.C: The standard does not require the matching of personal and client trades, so there is no rule that a client must first place a buy order before Rose may sell. What matters is that client transactions have priority and that the personal trade does not disadvantage clients, not that the two sides be paired.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), Priority of Transactions, a member's personal transaction that runs counter to a recommendation the member is currently giving clients is most likely:

options.A: a matter for the member alone.
options.B: justified by personal financial need.
options.C: barred as inconsistent with client advice.

rationales.A: Personal accounts are squarely within the scope of the standard, so a contrary trade is not the member's private affair. A member is a beneficial owner of any account he ultimately owns, controls, has the power to direct, or has a material interest in, and personal transactions in those accounts are covered by Standard VI(B). A contrary personal trade is therefore not free of constraint: it must rest on the member's own circumstances and must not disadvantage clients, and client transactions retain priority over it.
rationales.B: Sometimes members and candidates may need to enter a personal transaction that runs counter to current recommendations or strategies they are pursuing for client portfolios. For example, a member or candidate may be required at some point to sell an asset for personal financial reasons, and the sale may be contrary to the recommendations or advice the member or candidate is currently providing to clients. In such situations, members and candidates may be justified in acting counter to their advice to clients, provided client transactions keep their priority and no client is disadvantaged.
rationales.C: The standard is not an absolute bar, so divergence from the member's own advice is not what makes a personal trade impermissible. Personal circumstances such as a liquidity need can justify a transaction that is contrary to advice currently being given to clients. What the standard prohibits is letting a personal trade take precedence over client transactions or otherwise disadvantage clients.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), Priority of Transactions, a member's co-investment alongside clients in the same investment positions is most likely:

options.A: acceptable unless clients are disadvantaged.
options.B: free of conflict, since member and clients are aligned.
options.C: a conflict with clients, and prohibited as such.

rationales.A: The objective of the standard is to prevent personal transactions from adversely affecting the interests of clients or employers. A member or candidate having the same investment positions as clients, or being co-invested with them, does not always create a conflict; some clients in certain investment situations require members or candidates to have aligned interests. Personal investment positions or transactions of members or candidates or their firm should never, however, adversely affect client investments, so co-investment is acceptable precisely as long as that condition holds.
rationales.B: Alignment of incentives helps, but it does not remove the conflict. The co-invested member still has knowledge of pending client transactions and still trades in accounts he beneficially owns, so the duties of transaction priority and of disclosing the arrangement continue to apply. A co-invested manager can still advantage his own position at a client's expense, which is why the standard forbids personal positions that adversely affect client investments rather than treating alignment as a cure.
rationales.C: Co-investment is not prohibited. Holding the same positions as clients does not always create a conflict, and some mandates require the manager to have aligned interests. The standard targets personal positions or transactions that adversely affect client investments, not shared exposure as such.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), Priority of Transactions, money made by an adviser or mutual fund employee on personal investments is most likely:

options.A: ethical only if the gains are donated or disclosed.
options.B: ethical when no client is disadvantaged and rules are met.
options.C: unethical while the member is serving clients.

rationales.A: No donation requirement and no compensation-disclosure requirement of this kind exists. The three conditions in the guidance concern the client not being disadvantaged by the trade, the member not benefiting personally from trades undertaken for clients, and compliance with applicable regulatory requirements. Giving personal gains to charity, or reporting them to clients as a component of total compensation, is not what makes personal investing ethical.
rationales.B: Although conflicts of interest exist, nothing is inherently unethical about individual managers, advisers, or mutual fund employees making money from personal investments as long as (1) the client is not disadvantaged by the trade, (2) the member or candidate does not benefit personally from trades undertaken for clients, and (3) the member or candidate complies with applicable regulatory requirements. Transactions for clients must have priority over transactions in securities or other investments for which a member or candidate is the beneficial owner.
rationales.C: Personal investing is legitimate rather than forbidden, and serving clients does not suspend it. It is permitted whenever clients are not disadvantaged, the member derives no personal benefit from trades undertaken for clients, and applicable regulatory requirements are met. A prohibition on personal gain while in client service would go well beyond the standard, which is about the priority of client transactions rather than abstinence by the member.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), Priority of Transactions, trades for an account of which a member is a beneficial owner, though not the registered holder, are most likely:

options.A: permitted after clients and employers have had a chance to act.
options.B: permitted on the same terms as trades for any unrelated account.
options.C: permitted alongside client orders at matching prices.

rationales.A: Members or candidates may undertake transactions in accounts for which they are a beneficial owner only after their clients and employers have had adequate opportunity to act on a recommendation. Members and candidates are beneficial owners if they ultimately own, control, have the power to direct, or have a material interest in a security or investment, so the registered name on the account does not put its trades outside the standard. Personal transactions include those made for the member's or candidate's own account, for the accounts of immediate family members, and for accounts in which the member or candidate has a direct or indirect financial interest.
rationales.B: Whose name is on the account is not the test. Any account in which the member is a beneficial owner is covered, because beneficial ownership turns on ultimately owning, controlling, having the power to direct, or having a material interest in the investment. Family accounts, trusts, and entities in which the member holds such an interest are all within the standard, so their trades cannot be treated like trades for an account in which the member has no interest at all.
rationales.C: Trading at the same time as clients does not give clients and employers the adequate opportunity to act that the standard requires, and matching prices does not supply it either. The beneficially owned account must wait until after clients and employers have had their chance to act on the recommendation.

questions.stem: The purpose of Standard VI(B) of the Code and Standards is most likely to:

options.A: bar members from investing in securities they recommend to clients.
options.B: place client and employer interests ahead of personal interests.
options.C: create an administrative audit trail of members' personal trades.

rationales.A: The standard does not bar members from investing in the securities they cover or recommend. Personal investing is permitted, subject to transaction priority, disclosure of conflicts, applicable regulation, and firm policy. What the standard requires is precedence for clients and employers, not abstinence by the member.
rationales.B: Standard VI(B), Priority of Transactions, requires that members and candidates give the interests of their clients and employers priority over their personal financial interests. The standard is designed to prevent any potential conflict of interest, or the appearance of a conflict of interest, with respect to a member's or candidate's personal transactions. Conflicts between a client's interest and an investment professional's personal interest may occur, and when they do, client transactions must take precedence over transactions made on behalf of the member's or candidate's firm or personal transactions.
rationales.C: Reporting procedures such as pre-clearance, duplicate confirmations, and periodic holdings disclosure support compliance with the standard, but record-keeping is a means rather than the purpose. The substance of Standard VI(B) is the priority of transactions: clients first, then the employer, then the member.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), Priority of Transactions, a member who knows of a transaction pending for a client's account is most likely:

options.A: permitted to use that knowledge once the order is entered.
options.B: prohibited from benefiting from or conveying that knowledge.
options.C: bound only once the client's trade has been executed.

rationales.A: Entering the client's order does not release the member. A member with knowledge of a pending client transaction must neither benefit personally from it nor convey the information to others, so trading personally once the order is live is precisely the front-running the standard addresses. The client must have had adequate opportunity to act before the member transacts in an account he beneficially owns.
rationales.B: Standard VI(B) covers the activities of members and candidates who have knowledge of pending transactions that may be made on behalf of their clients or employers. Members and candidates are prohibited from benefiting from or conveying information about client transactions, which is what makes front-running a client order and tipping another party breaches of the standard rather than merely poor practice.
rationales.C: Pending transactions are the express subject of the standard, because that is where the front-running risk lives. A duty that attached only once the client's trade had been executed would leave uncovered the very window in which a member could trade ahead of a client or pass the information on.

questions.stem: Brady Securities, a broker/dealer, refers all prospective tax-exempt accounts to Lewis Brothers, an investment management firm. In return, Lewis Brothers makes its research available to Brady and directs stock commissions back to Brady. White, of Lewis Brothers, secures Maxwell as a new client through such a referral and says nothing about the arrangement. Under Standard VI(C), Referral Fees, White most likely:

options.A: owed no disclosure, as both firms gained from the referral.
options.B: owed the disclosure to Maxwell when the referral was made.
options.C: owed the disclosure to his employer, not to Maxwell.

rationales.A: Mutual benefit between the two firms does not cure the failure to inform the prospective customer of the referral compensation. Standard VI(C) requires members to disclose consideration received for the recommendation of products or services so that the client can judge the value of the referral and any partiality behind it. Research supplied to Brady plus commissions directed back to it is exactly such consideration, so an obligation to disclose existed.
rationales.B: White violated Standard VI(C) by failing to inform the prospective customer of the referral fee arrangement under which commissions were paid to Brady Securities. Such disclosure could have caused Maxwell's chief financial officer to reassess the Brady broker's recommendation and make a more critical evaluation of Lewis Brothers' services. The duty runs to the client or prospect at the time of the referral, and it extends to the nature and the value of the benefit.
rationales.C: Internal disclosure is not enough. The disclosure required by Standard VI(C) runs to the client or prospect being referred, so informing the employer's compliance department alone leaves the client unable to evaluate the referral. Firms commonly require internal approval of such arrangements as well, but that is an additional obligation rather than a substitute for telling the client.

questions.stem: Handley works in the trust department of Central Trust Bank and is paid for each client he refers to the bank's brokerage and personal financial management departments whenever the referral results in a sale. He refers several clients without mentioning the arrangement. Under Standard VI(C), Referral Fees, Handley most likely:

options.A: owed the disclosure to the clients he referred.
options.B: owed the disclosure to his employer, not to clients.
options.C: owed no disclosure, the payments being internal.

rationales.A: Handley violated Standard VI(C) by not disclosing the referral arrangement at Central Trust Bank to his clients. Standard VI(C) does not distinguish between referral payments paid by a third party for referring clients to the third party and internal payments paid within a firm to attract new business to a subsidiary; members and candidates must disclose all such referral fees. Handley is therefore required to disclose, at the time of referral, any referral fee agreement in place among Central Trust Bank's departments, and the disclosure must include the nature and the value of the benefit.
rationales.B: The disclosure duty under Standard VI(C) runs to clients, at the time of the referral, and it must cover the nature and value of the benefit received. Informing only the employer, which already knows because it created the arrangement, leaves the client unable to assess Handley's partiality in steering him toward an affiliated department.
rationales.C: Standard VI(C) does not distinguish internal interdepartmental payments from third-party referral fees; both must be disclosed to clients. That the compensation is paid within Central Trust Bank rather than by an outside party does not reduce Handley's incentive to refer, so the obligation to disclose remains.

questions.stem: Roberts asks her firm's trading desk to direct a large portion of client commissions to Naushon, a small broker/dealer run by a former classmate whose pricing is not competitive and whose research Roberts does not find useful. In return, Naushon recommends Roberts and her employer, Katama, to its wealthiest clients. Roberts tells no one of the arrangement. Under Standard VI(C), her disclosure duty most likely extends to:

options.A: no one, since routing commissions is a business judgment.
options.B: the wealthiest clients Naushon refers to her.
options.C: her employer Katama as well as the affected clients.

rationales.A: Directing commissions to a single broker can be defended as a business judgment, but that characterization does not extinguish the disclosure duty. What triggers Standard VI(C) is the reciprocal referral arrangement: Naushon steers its wealthiest clients to Roberts, and Roberts steers her clients' commission flow to Naushon. Any benefit given or received for the recommendation of services must be disclosed, so the duty runs to someone however the commission decision itself is labeled. The non-competitive pricing and the unused research are a separate loyalty problem, not a reason the disclosure duty disappears.
rationales.B: Standard VI(C) requires disclosure to the employer as well as to clients and prospective clients. Katama needs to know that its name is being promoted by a broker/dealer in exchange for commission flow, because that bears on how the firm's trading is directed and on the objectivity of the advice given in its name. Informing only the clients Naushon refers leaves both Katama and Roberts' own existing clients uninformed, so the disclosure would be incomplete.
rationales.C: Benefits given or received for the recommendation of services must be disclosed to clients, prospective clients, and employers, and the disclosure must come before entry into any formal agreement for services. Roberts therefore owes disclosure to Katama and to the clients whose commissions she is routing, as well as to those Naushon refers to her. Disclosure lets those parties weigh two things: any partiality shown in the recommendation — here, Roberts' incentive to route commissions to a classmate's firm and Naushon's incentive to recommend Roberts — and the full cost of the services. Telling no one leaves every affected party unable to make that judgment.

questions.stem: A state pension plan hires Arronski as a consultant to solicit and evaluate proposals from investment advisers, contracting with him to represent the plan's best interest in selecting a new manager. Arronski charges a fee to any investment manager he recommends that is subsequently awarded an allocation; he discloses that fee to the manager paying it and to no other party. Overseas, whose proposal best matches the plan's stated objectives, is selected and pays the fee. With respect to Standard VI(C), Arronski is most likely:

options.A: in compliance, since Overseas genuinely met the plan's objectives.
options.B: in violation, since the plan was never told of the fee.
options.C: in compliance, since Overseas was told of the fee it paid.

rationales.A: That Overseas genuinely met the plan's objectives does not cure the undisclosed, manager-paid fee. Standard VI(C) is concerned with the recipient's ability to judge the recommendation, not with whether the recommendation happens to turn out well. Withholding the fact that recommended firms pay Arronski once they are awarded business implies a potential lack of objectivity in the recommendation itself, and a suitable outcome does not retroactively supply the disclosure the plan was owed before it relied on his advice.
rationales.B: Arronski violated Standard VI(C) because he did not disclose the fee being paid by Overseas to the party relying on his recommendation. Withholding the information that firms pay him once they are awarded business based on his recommendations implies a potential lack of objectivity in his recommendation of Overseas. The plan contracted with him to represent its best interest in selecting a manager, so it is precisely the party that needed to know that the candidates he put forward would pay him if selected. Disclosure would have allowed the plan to evaluate any partiality in the recommendation and the full cost of the arrangement before acting on it.
rationales.C: Disclosure under Standard VI(C) runs to the client, prospective client, and employer — the parties relying on the recommendation — not to the manager paying the fee. Overseas already knew of the fee, since it was paying it, so telling Overseas conveyed nothing to the plan, which is the party whose judgment the disclosure is meant to inform. Telling the fee payer and no one else leaves the duty to the plan unperformed.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(C), disclosure of referral fees to a prospective client is most likely intended to:

options.A: ratify a fee arrangement the client has already accepted.
options.B: help the client weigh possible bias in the recommendation.
options.C: let the client request a discount on the service fees.

rationales.A: Disclosure is not an after-the-fact ratification of an arrangement the client has already accepted. Its purpose is to inform the decision to engage in the first place, which is why disclosure to a prospective client must be made before entering into a formal client relationship. A disclosure delivered once the client has committed arrives too late to serve either of the Standard's purposes, because the judgment it is meant to support has already been made.
rationales.B: Disclosure is intended to help the client weigh any possible bias in the recommendation of products or services. This is one of the two primary reasons for disclosing referral fees under Standard VI(C); the other is to allow clients and employers to evaluate the full cost of the services. Disclosure of referral fees must be made to clients, prospective clients, and employers so that they can judge both the possible bias in the recommendation and what they are actually paying in total.
rationales.C: Standard VI(C) does not require members or candidates to discount their fees when they receive referral fees, and the disclosure is not a mechanism for negotiating price. What the disclosure supports is the client's own evaluation: any possible bias in the recommendation of products or services, and the full cost of those services. Knowing the full cost may of course inform a client's decisions, but the Standard confers no right to a discount.

questions.stem: Appropriate disclosure of a benefit received for recommending services under Standard VI(C) is most likely required:

options.A: at any time before the first trade in the new account.
options.B: at any time before the first invoice is issued.
options.C: before entry into any formal agreement for services.

rationales.A: The trigger is the formal service agreement, which precedes both invoicing and trading, so a window that stays open until the first trade leaves the disclosure optional long after it matters. Tying disclosure to the first trade would let a client commit to the relationship, and to the fee structure behind it, without knowing that someone was compensated for the recommendation. Appropriate disclosure means that before entry into any formal agreement for services, the member or candidate informs the client or prospective client of any benefit given or received for the recommendation of services.
rationales.B: Disclosure must come before entry into any formal agreement for services, which is earlier than the first invoice, so a deadline set at the first invoice is too late. The timing matters because the disclosure is meant to inform the decision to engage, allowing the prospective client to evaluate any partiality in the recommendation and the full cost of the services before committing. By the time an invoice is issued, the client has already relied on the recommendation.
rationales.C: Appropriate disclosure means that before entry into any formal agreement for services, members and candidates must inform the client or prospective client of any benefit given or received for the recommendation of any services provided by the member or candidate. Placing the duty ahead of the agreement is what makes the disclosure effective: the prospective client can still weigh the possible bias in the recommendation and the total cost of the services while the decision to engage is open.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(C), a member who receives consideration for a referral must most likely disclose:

options.A: the arrangement in general terms, with further detail on request.
options.B: the arrangement apart from the fee's confidential commercial terms.
options.C: the nature of the consideration and its estimated dollar value.

rationales.A: A statement in general terms, with the particulars left for the client to ask about, does not let the client judge either partiality or full cost, and the Standard does not put the burden on clients to ask follow-up questions. The nature of the consideration must be disclosed — flat fee or percentage basis, one-time or continuing benefit, benefit based on performance, benefit in the form of provision of research, or other noncash benefit — together with its estimated dollar value. Structure, timing, and form are exactly the details that reveal how strong the incentive is.
rationales.B: Nothing in Standard VI(C) shields the consideration's commercial terms from the client whose referral generates them; confidentiality between the referring parties is not a defense against a disclosure duty owed to a third party. The member must disclose the nature of the benefit and its estimated dollar value, and consideration includes all fees, whether paid in cash, in soft dollars, or in kind.
rationales.C: The member or candidate must disclose the nature of the consideration or benefit — for example, flat fee or percentage basis, one-time or continuing benefit, benefit based on performance, benefit in the form of provision of research, or other noncash benefit — together with the estimated dollar value. Consideration includes all fees, whether paid in cash, in soft dollars, or in kind. Giving both the structure and an estimated value is what allows the recipient of the disclosure to gauge the size of the incentive behind the recommendation and the full cost of the services.

questions.stem: The purpose of disclosing referral fees under Standard VI(C) is most likely to allow:

options.A: referring brokers to document their claims to fees.
options.B: clients and employers to quantify the referring party's income.
options.C: clients and employers to judge partiality and total cost.

rationales.A: The protections run to clients, prospective clients, and employers, not to the referring party's commercial position, and documenting a fee claim between the referring parties is a private commercial matter. Members and candidates must inform their employer, clients, and prospective clients of any benefit received for referrals of customers and clients so that those parties can judge the recommendation they are being given. Securing the referring broker's own fee entitlement is not what the Standard is for.
rationales.B: The disclosure serves two purposes, not one. It allows clients and employers to evaluate any partiality shown in any recommendation of products or services, and to evaluate the full cost of the services. The estimated dollar value of the benefit is disclosed in service of those two evaluations, so reducing the requirement to a tally of the referrer's income misses the partiality purpose entirely.
rationales.C: Such disclosures allow clients and employers to evaluate (1) any partiality shown in any recommendation of products or services and (2) the full cost of the services. Members and candidates must inform their employer, clients, and prospective clients of any benefit received for referrals of customers and clients, and must also disclose when they pay a fee or provide compensation to others who have referred prospective clients to them. The duty therefore runs in both directions — fees received and fees paid — because either can bias a recommendation or add to what the client ultimately pays.

questions.stem: With respect to objectivity, Standard VI(A) most likely requires members and candidates to:

options.A: maintain objectivity solely when transacting for clients.
options.B: maintain objectivity in advice and in investment action.
options.C: discharge their objectivity duty through disclosure of conflicts.

rationales.A: This improperly narrows the duty to the execution of transactions. Objectivity is required both when rendering investment advice and when taking investment action, and advice is where a tainted judgment usually enters, since the client then acts on it. Investment advice or actions may be perceived to be tainted in numerous situations — for instance, when a member owns stock in the company that is the subject of a recommendation, or has a close personal relationship with the company's managers — and none of those circumstances distinguishes advising from transacting.
rationales.B: Members and candidates must maintain their objectivity when rendering investment advice or taking investment action. Investment advice or actions may be perceived to be tainted in numerous situations: for instance, a member or candidate may not be objective if he or she owns stock in the company that is the subject of an investment recommendation, or if the member or candidate has a close personal relationship with the company's managers. Requiring members and candidates to disclose all matters that reasonably could be expected to impair their objectivity when a conflict exists allows clients and prospective clients to judge motives and possible biases for themselves.
rationales.C: This reflects the misconception that disclosure substitutes for objectivity. The two requirements operate together: members and candidates must maintain their objectivity when rendering investment advice or taking investment action, and they must additionally disclose all matters that reasonably could be expected to impair that objectivity. Disclosure exists so that clients and prospective clients can judge motives and possible biases for themselves — not so that a disclosed bias becomes acceptable.

questions.stem: With respect to conflicts of interest, Standard VI(A) most likely requires members and candidates to:

options.A: take reasonable steps to determine whether conflicts exist.
options.B: defer to the compliance department's judgment on conflicts.
options.C: disclose only conflicts certain to influence their advice.

rationales.A: Members and candidates must take reasonable steps to determine whether a conflict of interest exists and disclose to clients any known conflicts of their firm. As an example, disclosure of broker/dealer market-making activities alerts clients that a stock purchase or sale might be made from or to the firm's proprietary account and that the firm has a special interest in the price of the stock. The duty is therefore active rather than passive: the member must look, including at the firm's own activities, and then disclose what that inquiry turns up.
rationales.B: The duty to inquire rests on the member or candidate personally, and deferring to the compliance function's judgment does not discharge it. Members must take reasonable steps themselves to determine whether a conflict of interest exists and must disclose to clients any known conflicts of their firm, such as broker/dealer market-making in a security being recommended. A compliance department may support and review that process, but it does not relieve the individual of the duty to look.
rationales.C: Certainty of influence is not the trigger. What must be disclosed are known conflicts, and more broadly all matters that reasonably could be expected to impair objectivity — a far lower threshold than a conviction that the conflict will in fact change the advice. Disclosure exists so clients and prospective clients can judge motives and possible biases for themselves, which they cannot do if the member first filters for conflicts he is sure about.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(A), whether a conflict of interest must be reported to the employer most likely turns on:

options.A: the monetary loss the conflict has caused the employer.
options.B: the conflict running to the employer rather than to clients.
options.C: the conflict's capacity to bias advice or harm the employer.

rationales.A: Reportability turns on interference with duties or bias, not on realized monetary loss. Reportable situations include conflicts that would interfere with rendering unbiased investment advice and conflicts that would cause a member or candidate to act not in the employer's best interest. Ownership of stocks analyzed or recommended, participation on outside boards, and financial or other pressures that could influence a decision are to be promptly reported so that their impact can be assessed before any loss occurs.
rationales.B: Conflicts that would interfere with rendering unbiased investment advice are expressly among the situations reportable to the employer; they are not set aside as a client-only concern. The same circumstances that generate conflicts to be reported to clients and prospective clients also dictate reporting to employers, because the employer needs to assess the impact and decide how the conflict should be resolved. Whom the conflict runs to is therefore not what decides reportability.
rationales.C: Reportable situations include conflicts that would interfere with rendering unbiased investment advice and conflicts that would cause a member or candidate to act not in the employer's best interest. The same circumstances that generate conflicts to be reported to clients and prospective clients also dictate reporting to employers. Ownership of stocks analyzed or recommended, participation on outside boards, and financial or other pressures that could influence a decision are to be promptly reported to the employer so that their impact can be assessed and a decision on how to resolve the conflict can be made.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(A), a disclosure of conflicts is most likely effective when it is:

options.A: standard in form and familiar to clients.
options.B: legally sufficient under the applicable rules.
options.C: prominent and written in plain language.

rationales.A: Familiarity is not the test. To be effective, disclosures must be prominent and must be made in plain language and in a manner designed to effectively communicate the information. Language that is standard in form, buried in a document and skimmed past, communicates nothing, so it fails the Standard however widely it is used and however readily clients recognize it. Members and candidates are responsible for determining how often, in what manner, and in what particular circumstances the disclosure of conflicts must be made.
rationales.B: The test is effective communication of the information to the recipient, not technical legal adequacy. A disclosure can satisfy every applicable rule and still fail Standard VI(A) if it is not prominent or not in plain language, because the purpose is to let clients and prospective clients judge motives and possible biases for themselves. That judgment requires comprehension, which is why the Standard speaks to how the information is conveyed rather than to whether a filing requirement has been met.
rationales.C: To be effective, disclosures must be prominent and must be made in plain language and in a manner designed to effectively communicate the information. Members and candidates are responsible for determining how often, in what manner, and in what particular circumstances the disclosure of conflicts must be made. Prominence and plain language together ensure the recipient actually receives and understands the conflict, which is the precondition for clients and prospective clients judging motives and possible biases for themselves.

questions.stem: Broker-sponsored limited partnerships formed to invest venture capital offer their issues to the public. Under Standard VI(A), the conflict-of-interest exposure these partnerships create is most likely:

options.A: present for the members who follow and promote the issues.
options.B: absent where the limited partners are passive.
options.C: confined to the general partner.

rationales.A: The potential for conflicts of interest also exists with broker-sponsored limited partnerships formed to invest venture capital. Members and candidates may be expected not only to follow issues from these partnerships once they are offered to the public but also to promote those issues in the secondary market after the public offering, which puts the research role and the marketing role in tension. Standard VI(A) requires a member in that position to resolve the potential conflict or to disclose it in accordance with the principles the standard sets out; the structure is not treated as conflict-free.
rationales.B: The passive role of the limited partners does not remove the conflict. The sponsoring broker's own economics create the conflict potential that the cross-departmental guidance flags expressly: its members may be expected to follow the partnership's issues once those issues are offered to the public and to promote them in the secondary market afterwards. Standard VI(A) requires that such situations be resolved or disclosed rather than assumed away.
rationales.C: The exposure is not confined to the general partner. Members and candidates who follow the partnership's issues once they are offered to the public, or who promote those issues in the secondary market after the offering, carry the same obligation to resolve the potential conflict or disclose it under Standard VI(A). Research and distribution roles are precisely the roles the cross-departmental guidance addresses.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(A), a member's ownership of stock in a company the member recommends to clients is most likely:

options.A: a conflict the standard ranks below board service at a covered company.
options.B: a holding the standard prohibits rather than requires to be disclosed.
options.C: the conflict the standard most often requires to be disclosed.
