rationales.A: Board service at a company the member covers is a conflict the standard addresses, but it is not the one the guidance identifies as most common. Standard VI(A) names ownership of stock in companies that members and candidates recommend to clients, or that clients hold, as the most prevalent conflict requiring disclosure, and nothing in the standard ranks board service above it.
rationales.B: Ownership is not prohibited. Prohibiting members and candidates from owning any such securities is the simplest method of preventing the conflict, but the guidance describes that approach as potentially overly burdensome and too restrictive. Sell-side best practice discourages such ownership and buy-side firms impose strict limits; in either case the beneficial ownership interest must be disclosed, so disclosure is not displaced by a ban.
rationales.C: The most prevalent conflict requiring disclosure under Standard VI(A) is members' and candidates' ownership of stock in companies that they recommend to clients or that clients hold. The simplest method for preventing such a conflict would be to prohibit members and candidates from owning any such securities, but the guidance treats that approach as potentially overly burdensome and too restrictive. The required response is therefore disclosure rather than prohibition, and it extends to any beneficial ownership interest in the securities or other investments the member recommends.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), the priority of client transactions relative to firm and personal transactions is most likely:

options.A: parity with the firm's own proprietary transactions.
options.B: precedence over firm and personal transactions.
options.C: a matter of each firm's own policy.

rationales.A: Client transactions and firm proprietary transactions do not rank equally. Client transactions take precedence over both transactions made on behalf of the member's or candidate's firm and the personal transactions of the member or candidate, so parity understates where the client sits in the queue.
rationales.B: Client transactions must take precedence over transactions made on behalf of the member's or candidate's firm or personal transactions. Standard VI(B) sets that hierarchy: clients come first, above both firm proprietary trading and the personal trading of the member or candidate, so neither a firm account nor a personal account may be filled ahead of a client for whom the security is suitable.
rationales.C: The ranking is not a matter of firm discretion. Standard VI(B) itself sets the hierarchy, placing clients first and ahead of both firm and personal interests; a firm's policies and procedures must implement that order rather than select a different one.

drills.los_text: recommend practices and procedures designed to prevent violations of the Code and Standards
drills.reading_name: Guidance for Standard VI: Conflicts of Interest

questions.stem: When a member cannot reasonably avoid a conflict of interest, the action required under Standard VI(A) is most likely to:

options.A: treat the client fairly and say nothing.
options.B: disclose the conflict clearly and completely.
options.C: withdraw from the engagement.

rationales.A: Proceeding in silence is itself the violation. Where avoidance is not reasonable, clear and complete disclosure of the conflict is necessary, and the member or candidate should also seek to mitigate the conflict to the extent possible and disclose how it has been mitigated. Fair treatment does not relieve the disclosure duty, because the client cannot assess the member's objectivity without knowing the conflict exists.
rationales.B: Best practice under Standard VI(A) is to avoid actual conflicts of interest and the appearance of them. When it is not reasonable for members and candidates to avoid a conflict, clear and complete disclosure of the conflict is necessary, and members and candidates should also seek to mitigate the conflict to the extent possible and disclose how the conflict has been mitigated. Avoidance is the first-best response; where it is not reasonable, the conflict is disclosed clearly and completely, mitigated so far as possible, and the mitigation itself disclosed.
rationales.C: Withdrawal is not mandated. The prescribed path for an unavoidable conflict is clear and complete disclosure, together with mitigation to the extent possible and disclosure of how the conflict has been mitigated; treating every unavoidable conflict as disqualifying goes beyond what the standard requires.

questions.stem: When reporting a conflict of interest to an employer, what a member must supply under Standard VI(A) is most likely:

options.A: a referral for the employer's own independent assessment.
options.B: notice that a conflict exists.
options.C: enough information to assess the conflict's impact.

rationales.A: The employer's assessment depends on the substance the member supplies. Members and candidates must give their employers enough information to assess the impact of the conflict; a referral stripped of detail leaves the employer unable to make that assessment and unable to apply its own guidelines to the situation.
rationales.B: A bare flag is insufficient. The employer must receive enough information to assess the conflict's impact, which means the facts bearing on its nature, size and persistence rather than a notification that something exists. By complying with employer guidelines, members and candidates allow their employers to avoid potentially embarrassing and costly ethical or regulatory violations, and the employer cannot apply those guidelines to a bare notice.
rationales.C: Disclosure of conflicts to employers may be appropriate in many instances, and when reporting conflicts of interest to employers members and candidates must give their employers enough information to assess the impact of the conflict. By complying with employer guidelines, members and candidates allow their employers to avoid potentially embarrassing and costly ethical or regulatory violations. The test under Standard VI(A) is sufficiency for the employer's own assessment of impact.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(A), a member's duty to report to the employer a conflict the member has been unable to resolve is most likely discharged:

options.A: by the disclosure already made to clients.
options.B: promptly.
options.C: at the next annual performance review.

rationales.A: Disclosure to clients does not substitute for the duty owed to the employer. Members and candidates should take reasonable steps to avoid conflicts, and where a conflict is not resolved they must report it to the employer promptly, whatever has already been said to clients. The two duties run in parallel, and discharging one does not discharge the other.
rationales.B: Members and candidates should take reasonable steps to avoid conflicts; if the conflicts are not resolved, Standard VI(A) requires that they report those conflicts promptly. Avoidance comes first, and an unresolved conflict is then reported promptly, so that the employer learns of the exposure while it can still act on it.
rationales.C: Deferring the report to a periodic review cycle fails the requirement. An unresolved conflict must be reported promptly rather than held for the next scheduled performance review, because the employer cannot manage or mitigate an exposure it does not yet know about.

questions.stem: Employer restrictions on personal trading and outside board membership are most likely:

options.A: broader than the Code permits an employer to impose on its staff.
options.B: aimed at actual conflicts rather than appearances.
options.C: appropriate to prevent the appearance of a conflict.

rationales.A: Firms legitimately restrict these activities, and members and candidates must comply with the restrictions. Nothing in the Code and Standards caps an employer's ability to limit personal trading, outside board membership and related activities; the guidance treats such limits as ordinary practice rather than as an overreach.
rationales.B: Preventing even the appearance of a conflict is the stated aim of these restrictions. They are directed at situations that might not normally be considered problematic from a conflict-of-interest point of view but that could nonetheless give the appearance of a conflict, so confining their reach to actual conflicts misses their purpose.
rationales.C: Many employers restrict personal trading, outside board membership and related activities to prevent situations that might not normally be considered problematic from a conflict-of-interest point of view but that could give the appearance of a conflict of interest. Standard VI(A) treats such restrictions as ordinary employer practice and requires that members and candidates comply with them, so the restrictions reach appearance-level exposures and compliance is itself an obligation of the member.

questions.stem: A member who provides investment services and also serves as a director of a covered company is most likely to be:

options.A: bound only by a confidentiality undertaking.
options.B: isolated from investment decision makers by firewalls.
options.C: isolated from investment decision makers only during merger talks.

rationales.A: An undertaking alone does not stop the flow of information. Where members and candidates providing investment services also serve as directors, they should be isolated from those making investment decisions by firewalls or similar restrictions; the structural separation, not a promise of confidentiality, is what manages the risk that material nonpublic information acquired through board service taints investment decisions.
rationales.B: Where members and candidates providing investment services also serve as directors, Standard VI(A) has them isolated from those making investment decisions by firewalls or similar restrictions. That insulation manages the risk that material nonpublic information acquired through board service reaches those who decide what the firm and its clients buy and sell.
rationales.C: The isolation is standing practice, not deal-contingent. Board service gives continuous access to material nonpublic information, so the firewall or similar restriction applies throughout the directorship rather than only while a transaction is under negotiation at the company.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(A), the parties entitled to full disclosure of actual and potential conflicts of interest are most likely:

options.A: clients, potential clients, and employers.
options.B: current clients.
options.C: employers, and clients on request.

rationales.A: Standard VI(A) protects investors and employers by requiring members and candidates to avoid or fully disclose to clients, potential clients, and employers all actual and potential conflicts of interest. Where a member or candidate has made full disclosure of an unavoidable conflict, the member's or candidate's employer, clients and prospective clients all have the information needed to evaluate the objectivity of the investment advice or action taken on their behalf. All three groups are express recipients.
rationales.B: Potential clients and employers are express recipients alongside current clients. A prospect needs the conflict information before engaging the member, because that is the moment at which the decision to rely on the member's advice is made; disclosure that waits until the relationship has begun comes too late to serve its purpose.
rationales.C: Clients do not have to ask. Clients, potential clients and employers all receive affirmative disclosure of actual and potential conflicts, so that each has the information needed to evaluate the objectivity of the investment advice or action taken on their behalf.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(A), how often and in what manner conflicts of interest are disclosed is most likely:

options.A: prescribed in detail by CFA Institute for all members.
options.B: set by each client in the advisory agreement.
options.C: determined by the member or candidate.

rationales.A: No schedule, format or wording is prescribed. Members and candidates are themselves responsible for determining how often, in what manner, and in what particular circumstances the disclosure of conflicts must be made, which is why the obligation is one of judgment rather than compliance with a template.
rationales.B: A client agreement may inform practice, but the judgment and the responsibility remain the member's. Standard VI(A) places the determination of frequency, manner and circumstances on the member or candidate, who must make it whether or not the advisory agreement speaks to the question.
rationales.C: Members and candidates are themselves responsible under Standard VI(A) for determining how often, in what manner, and in what particular circumstances the disclosure of conflicts must be made. The standard prescribes no schedule, so the member or candidate must exercise judgment consistent with the requirement that disclosures be prominent, in plain language, and effectively communicated.

questions.stem: An adviser is offered additional compensation by the promoter of a product the adviser recommends to clients. Under Standard VI(A), the adviser's best course of action is most likely to:

options.A: decline the additional compensation.
options.B: donate the payments to charity and continue the sales.
options.C: accept the compensation with prompt disclosure.

rationales.A: Standard VI(A) holds that best practice is to avoid actual conflicts of interest and the appearance of them. Where a conflict can be avoided rather than merely disclosed, avoidance is preferred, so the adviser's best course is to decline the promoter's offer of additional compensation altogether. Declining removes the incentive that would otherwise bias the recommendation, instead of leaving clients to weigh a bias they have been told about.
rationales.B: Redirecting the money to charity removes neither the incentive structure the promoter's payments create nor the client's need to know about the arrangement. The adviser is still being paid by the promoter on each sale, and the payment still sits between the adviser's recommendation and the client's interest. Declining the compensation addresses both problems at once.
rationales.C: Prompt and full disclosure is the minimum obligation once a conflict exists, and it is the right course where a conflict cannot be avoided. Here it can be: the illustrated best practice is avoidance, declining the additional compensation so that no conflict arises to be disclosed.

questions.stem: A research firm acquires an ownership interest in a company covered by one of its analysts. Under Standard VI(A), the firm's best practice is most likely to:

options.A: retain coverage of the security.
options.B: treat divestiture as the only available remedy.
options.C: discontinue coverage of the security.

rationales.A: Retaining coverage is not the best-practice response, and discontinuing it is not a disservice to research clients. When a new ownership interest creates a conflict of interest, discontinuing research coverage of the affected security avoids the conflict outright, which Standard VI(A) prefers to managing it. Clients are better served by no coverage than by coverage an ownership interest may bias.
rationales.B: Divesting the stake is one way to end the conflict, but it is not the only remedy and not the one the guidance illustrates. Discontinuing coverage of the affected security is the practical course; where coverage continues, the ownership interest must be disclosed to all clients instead.
rationales.C: When a new ownership interest creates a conflict of interest, best practice is to discontinue research coverage of the affected security. If coverage continues, the new relationship must be disclosed to all of the firm's clients, and the firm must also require the ownership interest to be disclosed to clients by its portfolio managers whenever they make specific investment recommendations or take investment action in that company's securities. Discontinuation avoids the conflict rather than merely disclosing it.

questions.stem: An analyst's personal holdings in an issuer conflict with a follow-up research report the analyst is due to write. Under Standard VI(A), best practice is most likely for the analyst to:

options.A: write the follow-up report as scheduled.
options.B: add a disclosure footnote to the report.
options.C: ask the employer to assign another analyst.

rationales.A: Writing the report on schedule leaves the conflict in place, and reassignment is the recommended course rather than an inappropriate one. Continuity of coverage does not outweigh avoiding a conflict that would otherwise colour every report written by the holder of the position, and the conflict here is ongoing rather than a one-off.
rationales.B: Disclosure is the fallback where a conflict cannot be avoided. Here it can be avoided: handing the follow-up report to a colleague who is not conflicted removes the conflict instead of asking clients to discount the analyst's conclusions on the strength of a footnote.
rationales.C: Best practice is to avoid the conflict by asking the employer to assign another analyst to draft the follow-up report. Reassignment to a colleague who is not conflicted is a widely used avoidance mechanism where personal or family holdings would otherwise require continuing disclosure and mitigation on every report the analyst produces on that issuer.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), the recommended practice with respect to an employer's personal-investing policies most likely calls for:

options.A: compliance without disclosure to clients.
options.B: confidential internal handling of the policies.
options.C: compliance and prominent disclosure to clients.

rationales.A: Compliance is only half of the recommended practice. Members and candidates must carefully consider the personal-investing policies applicable to their situation and comply with them, and they should then prominently disclose those policies to clients and prospective clients. Quiet adherence leaves clients unable to judge what protection they actually have.
rationales.B: Personal-investing policies bear directly on client trust, so they are not purely internal documents. The recommendation is prominent disclosure of them to clients and prospective clients, precisely because clients have an interest in knowing how the firm prevents conflicts in its employees' own trading.
rationales.C: Complying with an employer's policies and procedures designed to prevent potential conflicts of interest, and even the appearance of a conflict of interest, with respect to personal transactions is critical to establishing investor confidence in the investment industry. Because investment firms vary greatly in assets under management, types of clients, number of employees and so on, members and candidates must carefully consider the policies regarding personal investing that are applicable to their situation. They should then prominently disclose these policies to clients and prospective clients.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), participation in equity IPOs by investment personnel is most likely to:

options.A: create a conflict of interest for the member.
options.B: fall outside the firm's personal-trading restrictions.
options.C: be acceptable in an undersubscribed offering.

rationales.A: Purchases of initial public offerings by investment personnel create conflicts of interest in two principal ways. First, participation in an IPO may have the appearance of taking away an attractive investment opportunity from clients for personal gain, a clear breach of the duty of loyalty to clients. Second, personal purchases in IPOs may have the appearance that the investment opportunity is being bestowed as an incentive to make future investment decisions for the benefit of the party providing the opportunity. Members and candidates can avoid these conflicts, and the appearance of them, by not participating in IPOs; where a firm's policies do permit participation, they should preclear it, even in situations without any conflict between their participation and the client's interests. Members and candidates should not benefit from the position their clients occupy in the marketplace, whether through preferred trading, the allocation of limited offerings or oversubscription.
rationales.B: Allocation may be the broker's decision, but the conflict is the member's. IPO purchases by investment personnel raise both the appropriation-of-opportunity conflict and the appearance that the allocation is an incentive to direct future client business, which is why firms limit participation or require preclearance rather than leaving personal participation outside their personal-trading restrictions.
rationales.C: Both conflicts arise from who is buying and from the position the member's clients occupy in the marketplace, not from how heavily the issue is bid for, so they exist regardless of subscription levels. Oversubscription is one of the client positions a member should not benefit from, not the condition that creates the problem.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), an employer's authority over its investment personnel's acquisition of private placements most likely extends to:

options.A: requests that personnel abstain voluntarily.
options.B: disclosure of such purchases rather than limits.
options.C: strict limits on acquiring such securities.

rationales.A: That a placement is sold outside the public markets does not put it beyond the employer's reach. Participation in private placements raises conflict-of-interest issues similar to those surrounding IPOs, and employers may place strict limits on investment personnel acquiring securities in private placements rather than merely asking personnel to abstain.
rationales.B: The guidance expressly permits strict limits, not merely disclosure, on private-placement participation. The reason is that the transaction itself may be perceived as a favour or gift designed to influence future judgment or to reward past business deals, and disclosure after the fact does not remove that perception.
rationales.C: Employers may place strict limits on investment personnel acquiring securities in private placements. Participation in private placements raises conflict-of-interest issues that are similar to the issues surrounding IPOs. Investment personnel should not be involved in transactions, including but not limited to private placements, that could be perceived as favours or gifts that seem designed to influence future judgment or to reward past business deals.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), the recommended practice for preventing front-running of client trades is most likely:

options.A: blackout periods for personnel in the decision-making process.
options.B: annual written undertakings to avoid trading ahead of clients.
options.C: blackout periods limited to senior officers and portfolio managers.

rationales.A: Investment personnel involved in the investment decision-making process should comply with established blackout periods, so that managers cannot take advantage of their knowledge of client activity by front-running client trades, that is, by trading for one's personal account before trading for client accounts. The blackout period closes the window in which that knowledge could be exploited.
rationales.B: A written undertaking not to trade ahead of clients leaves the person who holds the conflicting information to police themselves, and it is tested only after a trade has happened. An established blackout period removes the opportunity structurally during the period when knowledge of pending client activity is valuable, so an annual certification does not achieve the same protection.
rationales.C: The practice covers investment personnel involved in the investment decision-making process, whatever their seniority. Involvement in that process, not rank, is what supplies knowledge of pending client trades, so a junior analyst inside the process is within the blackout and a senior officer outside it may not be.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), a member's personal-investing reporting obligation to an employer most likely covers:

options.A: executed trades but not standing holdings.
options.B: the disclosures a member chooses to volunteer.
options.C: trades, holdings and beneficial ownerships.

rationales.A: Reporting is not limited to executed transactions. Disclosure of holdings in which the employee has a beneficial interest is part of the framework, and firms may require that disclosure upon commencement of the employment relationship and periodically thereafter, because a standing position can conflict with client activity just as a new trade can.
rationales.B: Reporting is not a voluntary courtesy. Members and candidates must comply with their employer's reporting policies, and privacy is not a ground for declining to disclose personal holdings or beneficial ownerships that the policy covers.
rationales.C: Members and candidates must comply with their employer's reporting policies, which commonly include disclosure of personal holdings and beneficial ownerships, confirmations of trades supplied to both the firm and the employee, and preclearance procedures. Disclosure extends to holdings in which the employee has a beneficial interest, and firms may require it upon commencement of the employment relationship and periodically thereafter.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), duplicate confirmations of an employee's personal securities transactions are most likely:

options.A: ones a firm may require from the employee's broker.
options.B: satisfied by the employee's own trade reports.
options.C: barred by law from reaching the employer.

rationales.A: Firms may require employees to direct their brokers to supply the employer with duplicate copies or confirmations of all their personal securities transactions, together with copies of periodic statements for all securities accounts. The requirement has two purposes: it sends a message that there is independent verification, which reduces the likelihood of unethical behaviour; and it enables verification of the accounting of the flow of personal investments, which cannot be determined merely by looking at holdings.
rationales.B: Self-reporting is the thing the duplicates verify. Broker-supplied copies provide independent confirmation and, by signalling that such verification exists, deter misconduct in a way an employee's own account of their trading cannot. They also reveal the flow of personal investments, which a holdings report alone does not show.
rationales.C: No such bar exists. Employees can and routinely do direct their brokers to supply duplicate confirmations and periodic statements to the employer, and firms may require exactly that as a condition of personal trading.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), the recommended procedure for identifying conflicts raised by an employee's personal trading is most likely:

options.A: disclosure of all planned trades before execution.
options.B: review of personal trades after execution.
options.C: disclosure of planned trades in restricted names only.

rationales.A: Firms may require employees to disclose all planned personal trades so that the firm may identify possible conflicts prior to the execution of those trades. Preclearance procedures are designed to identify possible conflicts before a problem arises, rather than to document one after it has.
rationales.B: Review after the fact identifies a conflict that has already been acted on, and it cannot unwind a completed trade. Preclearance is preventive: disclosure of planned trades lets the firm identify the conflict before execution, which is the whole purpose of the procedure.
rationales.C: The procedure covers all planned personal trades, not only names on a restricted list. A conflict can arise in any security in which the firm is acting or about to act for clients, and the point of preclearance is that the firm, not the employee, decides which of those situations is a conflict.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), an investor's request for the firm's personal-investing policies is most appropriately met with:

options.A: a statement that they are confidential.
options.B: a boilerplate summary.
options.C: the policies themselves.

rationales.A: Responsiveness to such a request is the recommended practice, not refusal. Treating the firm's personal-investing policies as confidential withholds exactly the information that fosters an atmosphere of full and complete disclosure, and it leaves the investor unable to judge the conflicts of interest that personal trading creates.
rationales.B: On request the policies should be disclosed fully, and generic boilerplate defeats that purpose. Language such as "investment personnel are subject to policies and procedures regarding their personal trading" is expressly rejected, because it tells the investor nothing about how the firm actually controls personal trading. The disclosure has to provide helpful information to investors.
rationales.C: Upon request, members and candidates should fully disclose to investors their firm's policies regarding personal investing. The information about employees' personal investment activities and policies will foster an atmosphere of full and complete disclosure and address concerns about the conflicts of interest posed by personal trading. The disclosure must provide helpful information to investors; it should not be simply boilerplate language, such as "investment personnel are subject to policies and procedures regarding their personal trading." This is the disclosure-of-policies practice recommended under Standard VI(B).

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), front-running client trades is best described as trading for:

options.A: client accounts before disclosing a conflict to one's employer.
options.B: the firm's proprietary account after a research report is disseminated.
options.C: one's personal account before trading for client accounts.

rationales.A: This mischaracterizes front-running as a disclosure-timing issue between the member and the employer. Front-running is defined by the sequence of the trades themselves: the member's own account ahead of client accounts. Trading for client accounts is the obligation rather than the abuse, and when disclosure was made to the employer does not enter the definition.
rationales.B: This conflates front-running with proprietary trading and reverses the timing. Once a research report has been disseminated the information is public, so the informational advantage front-running exploits is already gone. Front-running is personal trading placed before client trades.
rationales.C: Front-running client trades means trading for one's personal account before trading for client accounts. Blackout and restricted periods exist for this reason: investment personnel involved in the investment decision-making process should comply with established blackout periods so that managers cannot take advantage of their knowledge of client activity by front-running client trades. The abuse is the use of advance knowledge of client order flow for personal benefit, ahead of the clients whose orders created it.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), the duplicate confirmation requirement for employees' personal trades is most likely intended to:

options.A: reconcile the firm's billing records.
options.B: signal independent verification.
options.C: monitor employees with prior violations.

rationales.A: The requirement signals independent verification, and that signal itself reduces the likelihood of unethical behavior, so the conduct dimension is the first of its two purposes. Reconciling the accounting of personal investments is the second purpose, and it is framed as enabling verification of the flow of employee investments rather than as a billing exercise.
rationales.B: The duplicate confirmation requirement has two purposes. First, it sends a message that there is independent verification, which reduces the likelihood of unethical behavior. Second, it enables verification of the accounting of the flow of personal investments, which cannot be determined from merely looking at holdings. Verification therefore serves both a deterrent function and a validation function for the flow of employee investments.
rationales.C: The deterrent operates firm-wide and prospectively, on everyone covered by the firm's personal-trading procedures. Limiting duplicate confirmations to employees with a disciplinary history would remove the message of independent verification for everyone else, which is where the deterrent does its work, and would leave the flow of their personal investments unverifiable.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), family accounts that are also client accounts are most appropriately:

options.A: given preferential allocations.
options.B: treated like any other firm account.
options.C: allocated after other client accounts.

rationales.A: Neither favoritism nor disadvantage is permitted: family accounts that are client accounts are treated like any other firm account. The reputational consequences a member may face with a relative are not a basis for preferential treatment, and preferring that account would breach the duty of fair dealing owed the firm's other clients.
rationales.B: Family accounts that are client accounts should be treated like any other firm account and should neither be given special treatment nor be disadvantaged because of the family relationship. If the member or candidate has beneficial ownership in a family account and the firm has preclearance and reporting requirements for personal transactions, the member or candidate may have to preclear the trades and report the transactions. The family relationship changes the personal-trading reporting that may apply, not the standard of care the account receives.
rationales.C: Disadvantaging a family client account breaches the duty owed it, because it is a client account first. Allocating to it systematically after other clients in order to preempt an appearance of favoritism is the mirror image of the prohibited conduct: the standard bars special treatment and disadvantage alike.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), compliance with an employer's personal-investing policies is most likely:

options.A: contingent on securities regulation.
options.B: discretionary.
options.C: obligatory.

rationales.A: Firm policies bind the member whether or not securities regulation duplicates them. The duty of loyalty to the employer under Standard IV(A) and the conflict-of-interest requirements of Standard VI(B) both require compliance with the firm's own personal-investing rules, so a policy with no regulatory counterpart, such as a firm blackout period, is still binding.
rationales.B: Compliance with the employer's established personal-investing policies is mandatory, not a matter the member may weigh against personal convenience. The policies exist to keep personal trading from competing with client interests, and treating them as guidance would leave that control to the discretion of the person it is meant to constrain.
rationales.C: Members and candidates must comply with their employer's personal investing policies, which could include limited participation in equity IPOs, restrictions on private placements, blackout and restricted periods, reporting requirements such as holdings disclosure, duplicate confirmations and preclearance procedures, and disclosure of policies. These are the compliance practices recommended under Standard VI(B), and following the ones the employer adopts is an obligation rather than a choice.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(C), the recommended practice for a member with respect to referral fee procedures is most likely to:

options.A: negotiate the terms directly with clients.
options.B: await procedures prescribed by securities regulators.
options.C: encourage the employer to develop procedures.

rationales.A: The recommended practice is to encourage the employer to develop referral-fee procedures, not to bypass the employer by settling terms with clients. Referral compensation is disclosable to the employer as well as to clients and prospective clients, and arranging it privately with a client removes the employer's ability to restrict the arrangement or require approval of it.
rationales.B: The guidance places the onus on the member to encourage employer-developed procedures, not on deferring to external regulation. Waiting for a regulator to prescribe procedures leaves the firm with no approval path and the member carrying an unmanaged conflict in the meantime; the obligation is a professional one that operates whether or not regulation addresses referral fees.
rationales.C: Members and candidates should encourage their employers to develop procedures related to referral fees. Employers may completely restrict such fees or outline the appropriate steps for requesting approval of a referral fee arrangement. This is the compliance practice recommended under Standard VI(C), and it places control of referral arrangements inside the firm's own procedures rather than leaving each member to handle them individually.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(C), updates to the employer on the amount and nature of a member's referral compensation are most likely due:

options.A: annually.
options.B: at approval of the arrangement.
options.C: quarterly.

rationales.A: The updates should be regular, meaning at least quarterly. An annual report tied to the compensation review cycle would leave the employer without a current picture of the amount and nature of referral compensation for most of the year, which is the information it needs in order to monitor the conflict it approved.
rationales.B: Approval initiates the reporting obligation rather than ending it: regular updates on the arrangements and the compensation received follow, at least quarterly. The conflict persists for as long as the arrangement does, and the amounts received change over time, so a single disclosure at the time approval is sought tells the employer nothing about what the program is actually paying.
rationales.C: Members and candidates who participate in approved referral fee programs should provide to their employer regular updates, at least quarterly, on the amount and nature of compensation received through referral fee arrangements. The obligation runs for the life of the arrangement: the employer approved the program on the basis of its terms, and only ongoing reporting of the amounts actually received lets it judge whether the conflict is still being managed.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(C), the consideration a member must disclose in a referral arrangement most likely includes fees paid:

options.A: in cash.
options.B: in cash, in soft dollars, or in kind.
options.C: in cash or in soft dollars.

rationales.A: Consideration expressly includes soft dollars and in-kind benefits, not just cash. Difficulty in valuing a noncash benefit is no ground for leaving it out: what must be disclosed is the nature and amount of the benefit, so a noncash benefit is described rather than priced. Confining disclosure to cash would let the whole economic substance of an arrangement be moved out of view.
rationales.B: Consideration includes all fees, whether paid in cash, in soft dollars, or in kind. The disclosure must cover the full economic substance of the arrangement, not just monetary payments, so research, services, equipment or other benefits received or given for a referral form part of what the employer, client and prospective client must be told about.
rationales.C: In-kind benefits are explicitly part of the consideration that must be disclosed. Research supplied in exchange for referrals affects the member's incentives exactly as a cash payment of the same value would, and consideration is defined to reach all fees, whether paid in cash, in soft dollars, or in kind.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(C), referral compensation must most likely be disclosed:

options.A: to the employer alone.
options.B: only for fees the member pays.
options.C: to the employer, clients, and prospective clients.

rationales.A: Clients and prospective clients are express recipients of the disclosure, alongside the employer. The disclosure exists so that the person deciding whether to engage the member can weigh the referral's effect on the recommendation, and that is a judgment only the client or prospective client can make; telling the employer and no one else leaves that person without the information.
rationales.B: Both directions of referral compensation are disclosable. Members and candidates must inform their employer, clients and prospective clients of any benefit received for referrals of customers and clients, and must also disclose when they pay a fee or provide compensation to others who have referred prospective clients to them. Compensation received is in fact the case in which the member's own recommendation is the thing being influenced, so it cannot be treated as private income.
rationales.C: Members and candidates must inform their employer, clients, and prospective clients of any benefit received for referrals of customers and clients. They must also disclose when they pay a fee or provide compensation to others who have referred prospective clients to the member or candidate. Both directions of referral compensation must be disclosed, because in each case the flow of money bears on whose interest the recommendation serves, and the parties relying on that recommendation are among those entitled to know.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(C), an employer's power to restrict a member's referral fee arrangements is most likely:

options.A: complete.
options.B: nonexistent.
options.C: limited to disclosure.

rationales.A: Employers may completely restrict referral fees or outline the appropriate steps for requesting approval of a referral fee arrangement. Members and candidates must comply with such employer restrictions and preapproval requirements, so the employer's power over these arrangements extends as far as prohibiting them outright.
rationales.B: Employers may completely restrict referral fees or define the approval path for them. A referral arrangement entered into in the course of the member's professional work is not a purely personal contract: it bears on the firm's clients and on the recommendations the firm makes, which is why the standard contemplates restriction and approval at the employer level.
rationales.C: Preapproval processes are legitimate governance that the member must follow. Employers may completely restrict referral fees or outline the appropriate steps for requesting approval of a referral fee arrangement, and the practice recommended to members is to encourage the employer to develop exactly such procedures. The employer's authority is therefore not confined to being told about an arrangement after the fact; it reaches requiring approval before the arrangement is entered into, and prohibiting it outright.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(C), the content required in a referral disclosure is most likely:

options.A: the name of the referring party only.
options.B: the nature of the benefit and its estimated dollar value.
options.C: the nature of the benefit, with unfixed amounts omitted.

rationales.A: Naming the referring party is not enough. The nature of the consideration or benefit — its structure, its duration and the form it takes — must be conveyed as well: whether it is a flat fee or on a percentage basis, one-time or continuing, based on performance, provided as research, or some other noncash benefit. The commercial terms are precisely the referred client's concern, because they are what reveal any partiality in the recommendation and what the client is ultimately paying.
rationales.B: The member or candidate must disclose the nature of the consideration or benefit — for example, flat fee or percentage basis, one-time or continuing benefit, benefit based on performance, benefit in the form of provision of research, or other noncash benefit — together with the estimated dollar value. Consideration includes all fees, whether paid in cash, in soft dollars, or in kind. Both elements are required: the nature of the benefit shows where the incentive lies, and the estimated dollar value shows the full cost of the services.
rationales.C: Where the amount is not fixed, an estimated value should be disclosed rather than nothing. The estimated dollar value is part of the required content of the disclosure, so omitting it on the ground that estimates are speculative leaves the client unable to evaluate the full cost of the services — one of the two purposes the disclosure exists to serve.

questions.stem: A referral fee agreement between two departments of the same firm, under Standard VI(C), is most likely:

options.A: disclosable only if it exceeds external referral rates.
options.B: disclosable like any third-party referral fee.
options.C: exempt from disclosure as an internal transfer.

rationales.A: Standard VI(C) sets no rate threshold. An internal referral benefit is disclosable on the same basis as an external one, whatever its size relative to what outside parties pay, because the conflict it creates does not depend on the amount. There is no comparison to external rates to be made before the duty to disclose arises.
rationales.B: Standard VI(C) does not distinguish between referral payments paid by a third party for referring clients to the third party and internal payments paid within a firm to attract new business to a subsidiary. Members and candidates must disclose all such referral fees, so any referral fee agreement in place among a bank's own departments must be disclosed to the referred client. The disclosure must include the nature and the value of the benefit, and it must be made at the time of the referral.
rationales.C: The standard does not distinguish third-party payments from internal payments between departments of the same firm. A payment made internally to attract new business to a subsidiary creates the same partiality in the recommendation, and adds to the same cost borne by the client, as a fee paid from outside. It must therefore be disclosed, with its nature and value, at the time of the referral.

questions.stem: Disclosure of referral fees under Standard VI(C) is most likely intended to:

options.A: standardize fee levels across the industry.
options.B: reveal any partiality and the full cost of services.
options.C: deter firms from entering referral arrangements.

rationales.A: Price standardization is not a purpose of Standard VI(C), and the standard does not address the level of fees at all. What it requires is that the client or employer be placed in a position to evaluate an arrangement the firm has already entered into; firms remain free to set the consideration as they see fit.
rationales.B: Such disclosures allow clients and employers to evaluate (1) any partiality shown in any recommendation of products or services and (2) the full cost of the services. These two purposes are the primary rationale for disclosure under Standard VI(C), and they explain the required content: the nature of the benefit speaks to partiality, and the estimated dollar value speaks to full cost.
rationales.C: Referral arrangements are legitimate under Standard VI(C); the standard regulates their disclosure, not their existence. The two purposes of disclosure are allowing the client or employer to evaluate any partiality shown in a recommendation and to evaluate the full cost of the services, neither of which is a deterrent aim.
